title: Why Office Satire Never Goes Out of Date
body:
Every generation thinks its workplace absurdities are new — open-plan then, 'culture decks' now — but the underlying comedy is constant: institutions rewarding the appearance of work over the substance of it. Satire works because readers recognise the meeting they sat in last Tuesday.

The trick in fiction is restraint. Exaggerate the systems, not the people. The moment a character becomes a cartoon, the reader stops seeing their own manager in him, and the satire loses its bite. Beating the System tries to keep every absurdity one memo away from real.

title: The Metric That Ate the Job
body:
Once a number becomes a target it stops measuring anything useful — Goodhart's law, and every workplace has a dozen examples. Response-time dashboards that punish thorough answers. Utilisation rates that reward booking meetings about meetings.

Fiction can do what management books can't: show the human cost in a single scene. The employee who has learned exactly which numbers to feed the machine, and what it has done to the part of him that once cared about the work.

title: Writing the Villain Who Is Just Doing Their Job
body:
Corporate fiction rarely needs a villain, because the system supplies one for free. The most unsettling antagonist is the pleasant middle manager who genuinely believes the restructuring is for everyone's benefit — and who, in a different job, would be a good person.

The reader's discomfort comes from recognising that the manager is not lying. That sincere belief in the process is what makes the machine run, and what makes a novel about it more than a complaint.
